items.title: Jon-Erik Kellso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: We actually had a big band when I was in fifth grade and he was in sixth grade, playing big band classics.

ctx.x: Yeah. Sometimes you talk it over beforehand, sometimes you don’t. Sometimes you’re just on the stand and you’d better to know the song they call or else you’re going to be embarrassed or you’re going to be scuffling a little bit. And for the trumpet player it’s a little bit more pressure than the other guys in the band, because the trumpet player is generally expected to play the melody, at least so they can recognize it. And so I mean if you’re the clarinet player in the front line, playing sort of ensemble,…

under interesting circumstances, because starting out as young as I did, my first big job — major, steady gig — was playing at a place called Greenfield Village in Dearborn, Michigan, which is where the Henry Ford Museum is. And my friend Mike Karoub, who I mentioned before, he always had a lot of chutzpah you know. And aside from being a great player, he was very ambitious, that may be a better word for it. But he decided, we had started playing around at PTA meetings, playing Dixieland arrangements that his…
No one’s mother would let them come to rehearsal.
